newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein welcomes special status with U.S.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein welcomes special status with U.S.

text.p: King Hussein of Jordan on Tuesday welcomed an announcement by U.S. President Bill Clinton naming his country a major non-NATO ally of the United States.

"We are proud of this and we appreciate this initiative by the U.S. president and his administration," the king said in a letter to his army and security chiefs carried by the official Petra news agency.
Clinton last week named Jordan a major non-NATO ally, adding the country to a small group of states granted priority to receive excess U.S. materiel and other military privileges.
A U.S. state department official said at the time he did not believe the designation carried with it any expanded U.S. commitment to come to Jordan's defence in a time of crisis.
But the king said Jordan "realised that allies owe it to each other to work together on the basis of mutual respect and joint cooperation...and in confronting any event or new emergency."

The king said former Warsaw Pact countries were scrambling to join NATO "to enjoy what has been afforded to us now", and condemned those he said were questioning Jordan's need to safeguard its military strength. "Pity on those who want Jordan small and weak eternally," he said.

U.S. relations with Jordan plummeted during the 1991 Gulf War when the kingdom was seen as sympathetic to Iraq. But ties improved dramatically after Jordan signed a peace treaty with Israel in October 1994.
Since then Washington has taken several steps to strengthen ties with Jordan, including the transfer of F-16 warplanes to Jordan's armed forces.
Other countries which have been granted the special status are Australia, Egypt, Israel, Japan and the Republic of Korea.
